podcast.title: The night before the exam

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you study a little every day, or a lot the night before? Guess: who almost dropped out of university — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today we're going back to school — the topic is education.
Sam, be honest. What kind of student were you?
[chuckle] The last-minute kind. I always started to revise the night before the exam. Coffee, three a.m., panic.
And did it work?
Sometimes. But at university it stopped working. I missed one deadline, then another, and in my first year I almost had to drop out.
Really? What changed?
A teacher sat down with me and showed me how to plan. I had to learn the ropes — how to study, not just what to study.
That's a good teacher. I was the opposite. I hit the books every day, even on holiday.
Of course you did. [laugh]
And I got a scholarship, so I didn't have to pay tuition. That was a big help for my family.
Well done. Do you think school has changed since we were kids?
A lot. When I was at school, the curriculum was mostly facts. Learn the dates, write them down, forget them.
And now?
Now good schools teach critical thinking — asking questions, checking information, not believing everything you read online.
That's so important today. And it's not only reading and writing. Digital literacy matters too.
Okay, tips for our listeners who are studying English. Mine: a little every day is better than a lot once a week.
And mine: test yourself. Close the book and try to say it, or write it. That's how it stays in your head.
Like speaking in a SpeakLab call, actually.
Exactly. You don't need to be perfect. You need to practise. Then you'll pass with flying colours.
Here's your question for your next call: who was your best teacher, and what did they do differently?
Mine changed my life. See you next time!
Bye for now!
